observation.visible_scene: A fixed close-up of a hydraulic press: a large polished metal piston head is suspended above a short cylindrical anvil painted with diagonal yellow-and-black hazard stripes. A heap of white shattered fragments rests on the anvil's top face, and many more white shards litter the surrounding metal table. Vertical yellow-and-black striped guard columns flank the scene on left and right, and a small action camera on a mount is visible at the far left. The camera and background do not move across the clip.
visible_changes: At t=0 a cloud of white fragments is already airborne between the raised press head and the anvil; through roughly t=0.5–0.6 these pieces fall and settle onto the heap, with motion-blurred shards continuing to streak down the front face of the anvil.

From t=0 to about t=1.5–2.0 the press head holds a constant raised height (a static interval); during this time the shard heap on the anvil sits mostly still, with only occasional small pieces bouncing or drifting.
From about t=2.0 onward the press head begins a slow, continuous downward descent, steadily closing the gap above the heap.

Near t=2.8–3.2 the descending head makes contact with and compresses the heap; the top of the white pile is visibly lowered and small white fragments are ejected sideways (left and right) as motion-blur streaks.

The anvil, the horizontal position of the press head, the side columns, the mounted camera, and the shards scattered on the table remain in the same positions throughout, indicating object motion (head descent, fragment settling/ejection) rather than camera motion.
outside_clip_unknowns: The earlier event that shattered the object and launched the airborne fragments seen at t=0 (the impact itself is before the crop).
Whether the press will continue to crush the heap fully after t=3.2, and the final state of the fragments.
What the original object was before it was broken into the white shards.
uncertain_details: The material of the white fragments (porcelain, ceramic, plastic, etc.) cannot be confirmed from the images.
The exact moment the press head first touches the heap, and whether its descent is perfectly smooth or stepped, is hard to pin down from the sampled frames.
The precise height of the press head in the early frames is only estimated; small vertical drift cannot be ruled out.
